verses.text: Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted.
Just as many were appalled at Him—His appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man, and His form was marred beyond human likeness—
so He will sprinkle many nations. Kings will shut their mouths because of Him. For they will see what they have not been told, and they will understand what they have not heard.
Who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?
He grew up before Him like a tender shoot, and like a root out of dry ground. He had no stately form or majesty to attract us, no beauty that we should desire Him.
He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised, and we esteemed Him not.
Surely He took up our infirmities and carried our sorrows; yet we considered Him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted.
But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.
We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all.
He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth. He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth.
By oppression and judgment He was taken away, and who can recount His descendants? For He was cut off from the land of the living; He was stricken for the transgression of My people.
He was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death, although He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth.

Yet it was the LORD’s will to crush Him and to cause Him to suffer; and when His soul is made a guilt offering, He will see His offspring, He will prolong His days, and the good pleasure of the LORD will prosper in His hand.
After the anguish of His soul, He will see the light of life and be satisfied. By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities.

Therefore I will allot Him a portion with the great, and He will divide the spoils with the strong, because He has poured out His life unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors. Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.

prophecies.why_christians_read_it_this_way: The passage describes a servant who is innocent, is rejected, is struck down for other people's wrongs, is counted among sinners, dies and is buried, and yet afterward 'sees his offspring' and is exalted. Philip uses it to explain Jesus to the Ethiopian official in Acts 8, and Peter builds on it in 1 Peter 2. Christians see in it the clearest Old Testament picture of a death that pays for others.
prophecies.traditional_jewish_reading: The most common Jewish reading, associated with Rashi and later medieval commentators, takes the servant as the people of Israel, who are called God's servant elsewhere in Isaiah (41:8; 49:3). On this view the speakers in chapter 53 are the nations, who come to realize that Israel's suffering in exile was not what they assumed. Some older rabbinic sources did apply parts of the chapter to the Messiah (for example a passage in the Talmud, Sanhedrin 98b), so the individual reading has Jewish history too. The Aramaic Targum Jonathan reads Isaiah 52:13 as 'My servant the Messiah', but it applies only the servant's exaltation to the Messiah; the suffering in chapter 53 it applies to others, such as Israel. Jewish teachers today often point to details they say do not fit Jesus, such as 'he will see offspring and prolong his days.'
prophecies.traditional_jewish_reading_status: Paraphrased in our own words; not quoted. Checked by John (2026-10-26) against the linked sources. Jewish sources are link only.
prophecies.note: Whether the servant is an individual or Israel is the central debate. Christians usually answer that in 53:8 the servant suffers 'for the transgression of my people', which separates him from the people, and that Isaiah 49:5-6 has the servant restoring Israel.

ot.text_source: site/data/bible/bsb.json (team copy of bereanbible.com/bsb.txt; matched against independent download)

verses.text: Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.

nt.text_source: site/data/bible/bsb.json (team copy of bereanbible.com/bsb.txt; matched against independent download)

verses.text: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet:
“Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”).

prophecies.why_christians_read_it_this_way: Matthew sees the virgin birth as the full meaning of the sign given to the house of David: a child whose name means 'God with us.' Isaiah 7-11 goes on to describe a child who rules on David's throne (9:6-7; 11:1-10), so many Christians read the sign as reaching beyond Ahaz's own time. Conservative scholars also note that almah is never clearly used in the Hebrew Bible of a married woman.
prophecies.traditional_jewish_reading: Jewish interpreters read the verse as a sign for King Ahaz in his own day: a young woman already known to him would have a son, and before the boy was old enough to choose between good and bad, the two kings threatening Judah would be gone (7:16). The Hebrew word almah means a young woman, and the usual word for virgin is betulah. The child is often identified as a son of Ahaz (such as Hezekiah) or of the prophet.
prophecies.traditional_jewish_reading_status: Paraphrased in our own words; not quoted. Pending John's check. Jewish sources are link only.
prophecies.note: Matthew follows the Greek Septuagint, which had already translated almah as parthenos ('virgin') before Jesus was born. A 'near and far' (dual) fulfilment reading is common among Christian scholars.
